title: ELKANAH HAD TWO WIVES—One Had Children, the Other Was Tormented for Having None
paragraphs: ELKANAH HAD TWO WIVES—One Had Children, the Other Was Tormented for Having None

One woman walked into the house with children around her feet. The other walked in carrying an emptiness nobody could see. Then the woman who already had what Hannah desperately wanted began tormenting her because she did not have it.
There are some Bible stories we have heard so many times that we accidentally clean them up.
We turn them into inspirational quotes.
We skip over the uncomfortable sentences.
We rush toward the miracle because sitting inside the pain makes us uncomfortable.
But 1 Samuel 1 does not begin with a miracle.
It begins with a complicated home.
A husband.
Two wives.
Children.
Jealousy.
Provocation.
Tears.
A woman who could not eat.
A woman praying so desperately that a priest thought she was drunk.
And somewhere inside that scandalous, painful household was a woman named Hannah whose tears were about to become part of one of the most consequential stories in Israel.
But before Samuel ever cried in his mother's arms...
Hannah cried without him.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Not at the miracle.
At the waiting.
Elkanah had two wives.
Scripture says:
“He had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.” — 1 Samuel 1:2, KJV
That last sentence lands with almost brutal simplicity.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah had none.
The Hebrew names the women plainly:
חַנָּה — Ḥannah
פְּנִנָּה — Peninnah
And the text immediately establishes the wound around which much of the chapter will turn.
One had what the other desperately wanted.
Before going any further, we need to say something the passage itself requires us to understand carefully.
The Bible's description of Elkanah having two wives is not the same thing as God's endorsement of polygamy.
Scripture often tells us truthfully what human beings did without declaring everything they did to be God's design.
Jesus points us back to creation itself when speaking about marriage: “the two shall become one flesh” (Matthew 19:4–6; compare Genesis 2:24).
And throughout the Old Testament, households fractured by multiple wives repeatedly reveal rivalry, grief, favoritism, and conflict.
Elkanah's household was no exception.
Every year he traveled from Ramah to Shiloh to worship and sacrifice to the LORD.
And when the time came to distribute portions from the sacrifice, Scripture tells us that he gave portions to Peninnah and her sons and daughters.
Then comes Hannah.
“But unto Hannah he gave a worthy portion; for he loved Hannah: but the LORD had shut up her womb.” — 1 Samuel 1:5, KJV
The Hebrew text contains a famously difficult expression:
מָנָה אַחַת אַפָּיִם — mānāh ʾaḥat ʾappāyim
Translations handle the phrase differently. The KJV has “a worthy portion,” while many modern translations understand it as some form of special or double portion.
The precise expression is debated.
The emotional point is not.
Elkanah loved Hannah.
And Hannah was hurting.
Love did not make the infertility disappear.
A special portion did not silence the ache.
And perhaps somebody reading this understands that more deeply than anyone around you realizes.
People can love you...
and still be unable to fix what hurts.
Someone can put an arm around you and still not understand what happens when the bedroom door closes.
They can tell you how blessed you are.
They can remind you of everything you still have.
They can genuinely mean well.
And still...
there is that empty chair.
That unanswered prayer.
That pregnancy test.
That diagnosis.
That relationship that never came.
That child who walked away.
That marriage you prayed would heal.
That opportunity everyone else seems to receive effortlessly.
That prayer you have whispered so many times that sometimes you wonder whether you have any words left.
And then there is the additional pain nobody asked for:
watching somebody else receive what you have been begging God for.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.
But the story gets worse.
Peninnah did not simply enjoy her blessing.
She weaponized Hannah's wound.
First Samuel 1:6 says:
“And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the LORD had shut up her womb.”
Listen to the Hebrew:
וְכִעֲסַתָּה צָרָתָהּ גַּם־כַּעַס
ve-khiʿasattāh tsārātāh gam-kaʿas
The language communicates intense provocation and vexation. Peninnah is described in relation to Hannah as her rival, and the text portrays repeated, deliberate provocation.
Not accidental insensitivity.
Not one careless comment.
This happened repeatedly.
Year after year.
Imagine it.
Hannah was already carrying grief inside her own body.
Then someone kept touching the bruise.
She did not need Peninnah to remind her that she was childless.
She knew.
She woke up knowing.
She went to sleep knowing.
And perhaps the cruelest wounds are sometimes not the wounds themselves...
but the people who discover where you bleed and keep pressing there.
Maybe someone has done that to you.
They know about your past, so they bring it up when they want to humiliate you.
They know your marriage is struggling, so they parade theirs in front of you.
They know you are lonely, so they make jokes about your singleness.
They know you are recovering, so they keep naming the person you used to be.
They know your child is struggling.
They know your finances collapsed.
They know you failed.
They know you relapsed.
They know you are ashamed.
And somehow your wound became their weapon.
But listen carefully:
Your wound is not your name.
Your waiting is not your identity.
Your humiliation does not get the final sentence.
Hannah's story had not ended simply because Peninnah thought she understood it.
And neither has yours.
Scripture says the provocation continued year after year until Hannah wept and would not eat.
Elkanah saw her.
And like many people who love someone they cannot fully understand, he tried to comfort her:
“Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?” — 1 Samuel 1:8, KJV
There is something painfully human about that question.
Elkanah loved her.
But love does not always equal understanding.
He was essentially saying, “You have me.”
Hannah's heart was saying, “But you are not what I am grieving.”
Sometimes people try to make suffering disappear by reminding us of other blessings.
And gratitude matters deeply.
But biblical faith does not require pretending grief does not exist.
Jesus Himself wept.
The Psalms are filled with lament.
Faith can worship while crying.
Faith can trust while hurting.
Faith can say, “God is good,” while simultaneously asking, “How long, O LORD?”
Hannah finally did something with her pain that Peninnah could never prevent.
She took it somewhere Peninnah could not follow.
Into the presence of God.
First Samuel says Hannah was in “bitterness of soul.”
The Hebrew expression is:
מָרַת נָפֶשׁ — marat nāfesh
Deeply bitter in soul.
She was not strolling casually into prayer.
She was shattered.
“And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.” — 1 Samuel 1:10, KJV
Do not miss this.
Hannah did not wait until she became emotionally presentable before approaching God.
She brought Him the wreckage.
The tears.
The disappointment.
The unanswered questions.
The longing.
The bitterness.
She prayed from inside it.
Somebody needs permission to do that again.
You do not have to sanitize your tears before bringing them to Jesus.
You do not need Christian vocabulary impressive enough to hide how exhausted you are.
You do not need to tell God you are fine when you are falling apart.
He already knows.
Prayer is not performing strength before God.
Prayer is coming because you know you need Him.
Hannah poured herself out so intensely that her lips moved while her voice could not be heard.
Eli the priest watched her and reached the wrong conclusion.
He thought she was drunk.
Think about that.
Hannah was already misunderstood at home.
Now she was misunderstood at the place of worship.
She was hurting...
and the spiritual leader in the room initially misread her pain.
Maybe you know what that feels like too.
Sometimes the person barely holding themselves together is mistaken for being distant.
Difficult.
Cold.
Unspiritual.
Unfriendly.
Weak.
Maybe nobody knows the battle taking place underneath your silence.
Eli told her to put away her wine.
Hannah answered:
“No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit... but have poured out my soul before the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 1:15, KJV
There it is.
One of the most beautiful descriptions of prayer in Scripture.
I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
Not polished it.
Not edited it.
Not disguised it.
Poured it out.
There are moments when prayer sounds less like a sermon and more like:
“Jesus, help me.”
“Lord, I don't understand.”
“Father, I'm tired.”
“God, please don't let me become bitter.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
And heaven is not offended by the broken prayer of a broken person coming honestly before God.
Hannah made a vow concerning the son for whom she prayed, promising that if God gave her a son, she would give him to the LORD.
Eventually Scripture says:
“And the LORD remembered her.” — 1 Samuel 1:19, KJV
That phrase does not mean God had forgotten Hannah and suddenly remembered she existed.
In biblical language, God's “remembering” often signals His movement toward someone according to His covenant purposes.
Then Hannah conceived.
She bore a son.
She called him Samuel.
The text connects his name with her declaration:
“Because I have asked him of the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 1:20, KJV
Imagine holding the child you once cried over before he even existed.
Imagine looking into the face of an answered prayer.
But we must be careful here.
Hannah's story is not permission to tell every grieving woman, “If you pray hard enough, God will give you a baby.”
It is not a formula.
Scripture never gives us the right to turn one person's miracle into a guarantee God has made to everybody.
Some prayers receive the answer we desperately wanted.
Some receive an answer we never expected.
Some remain unanswered in the way we hoped throughout this earthly life.
Christian hope ultimately rests somewhere greater than getting the earthly outcome we desire.
It rests in God Himself.
And ultimately, it rests in Jesus Christ.
Because the Bible is not fundamentally the story of human beings discovering techniques for obtaining their dreams.
It is the story of the holy God redeeming sinners.
And that story leads us to Christ.
Hannah received Samuel.
But humanity needed something infinitely greater.
We needed a Savior.
We had a problem deeper than infertility, loneliness, rejection, poverty, sickness, disappointment, or humiliation.
We had sin.
And no amount of self-improvement could remove our guilt before a holy God.
Then Jesus came.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He touched the rejected.
He welcomed the broken.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called sinners to repentance.
He carried the cross.
And on that cross, Christ bore sin and suffered in the place of sinners.
Then He rose from the grave.
That is the Gospel.
Not that Christians always get the ending they requested.
But that in Christ, sin and death do not get the final word.
Grace does.
Hannah's humiliation was not the final chapter of Hannah.
Peter's denial was not the final chapter of Peter.
The thief's criminal past was not the final chapter of the thief who turned to the crucified Christ.
And if you belong to Jesus, your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending.
That authority belongs to Christ.
Maybe your scandal is something everybody knows.
Maybe yours is hidden.
Maybe your story contains sexual sin.
Addiction.
Pride.
An affair.
A broken marriage.
A secret habit.
Years of pretending.
Bitterness.
Abortion.
Greed.
Pornography.
Dishonesty.
Religious hypocrisy.
Or perhaps you were the one wounded by somebody else's sin, and now bitterness is slowly building a home inside you.
Do not confuse grace with pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost Jesus blood.
The Gospel calls us to repentance.
To turn.
To stop defending what Christ died to save us from.
To come into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
You do not need another mask.
You need Jesus.
You do not need a better reputation while your soul dies quietly behind it.
You need Jesus.
You do not need everyone on Facebook believing you have everything together.
You need Jesus.
And perhaps the deepest question in Hannah's story is not simply:
“When will my prayer finally be answered?”
Maybe another question is:
“What will I do with my heart while I wait?”
Will pain make you run from God...
or pour yourself out before Him?
Will somebody else's blessing become your bitterness?
Will somebody else's cruelty determine who you become?
Will your unanswered prayer become evidence, in your mind, that God has abandoned you?
Or will you bring the questions, tears, anger, confusion, repentance, and longing into His presence?
Hannah went into worship carrying something she could not fix.
And she poured out her soul.
Maybe today that needs to be you.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
Let believers who see those words pray instead of judge.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only person crying behind a smiling profile picture.
Not to expose them.
To remind them:
“You are not alone.”
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But if biblical truth has strengthened you, sharing it is one simple way you can put that truth in front of somebody who may desperately need it tonight.
There may be a husband who cannot understand why his wife keeps crying.
There may be a Peninnah who needs to repent because she has been using another person's weakness to make herself feel powerful.
There may be someone who has not prayed honestly in years.
Your share could place Scripture in front of them.
Not so we can build an impressive number on a screen.
So more people can encounter Scripture.
So wounded people can hear about grace.
So comfortable hearts can be confronted with repentance.
So sinners can hear that forgiveness is available through Jesus Christ.
So people who believe their story is already ruined can discover that the cross says otherwise.
Because there may come a night when you become Hannah again.
A night when somebody else's life seems full while yours feels painfully empty.
A night when someone presses the bruise.
A night when even people who love you cannot understand you.
A night when your prayer is barely audible.
Come back and remember:
Hannah was not invisible to God.
But do not stop at Hannah.
Look beyond Shiloh.
Look toward Calvary.
There you find the greater evidence that suffering does not mean God is absent.
There you find Jesus rejected, mocked, wounded, crucified...
and then the empty tomb.
The Christian story moves through death toward resurrection.
Through repentance toward forgiveness.
Through guilt toward grace.
Through the old life toward new creation in Christ.
So bring Him the chapter you wish had never been written.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the waiting.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the sin—and repent.
Bring Him the tears.
Bring Him the parts of your story you thought disqualified you forever.
Because the Gospel does not tell us that our past was insignificant.
It tells us something far more astonishing.
Jesus Christ is greater.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you after everything else fades is this:
The place where you thought your story was over may become the very place where grace teaches you that Jesus still holds the pen.
